claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has been produced in a hierarchical-heterostructured state with multilevel chemical fluctuations and phase heterogeneities.
Machine learning can predict mechanical properties of single-phase and multiphase alloys with reasonable accuracy.

Combining high-resolution microstructural descriptors with a limited set of ab initio descriptors can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 within ±10% of experiment.
The proposed model will be more than 10 times faster than full-scale CALPHAD and density-functional-theory approaches.

First-principles calculations can provide physical inputs such as elastic constants, misfit volumes, surface energies, and unstable stacking-fault energies for physics-based mechanical-property models.
A limited number of calculations on representative microstructural motifs can replace full-scale ab initio or CALPHAD calculations while retaining predictive accuracy.
Composition gradients, phase-fraction distributions, and nanoscale chemical ordering mediate the relationship between hierarchical structure and bulk mechanical response.
Local stiffness variability governs the macroscopic Young's modulus and contributes to the plastic response of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Defect distributions govern the yield strength and fracture toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Physics-based descriptors preserve model interpretability while maintaining predictive accuracy.
Explicit first-principles evaluation of fracture strength or yield strength in alloys is mostly beyond available DFT implementations.
First-principles simulations remain challenging for disordered multi-principal-element alloys.
CALPHAD-based methods have high computational demands and limited ability to predict fracture toughness in complex heterogeneous alloys.
Standalone machine-learning methods require large training sets and therefore have high computational demands.
The method will cease to be reliable when imaging resolution fails to capture mechanically critical heterogeneity scales.
Unexpected phases, extreme anisotropy, or other departures from the training domain will make the limited physics descriptors inadequate.
Fracture-toughness predictions are especially uncertain because fracture measurements are sensitive to local defects and microstructural inhomogeneity.

contradictions.description: The claimed accuracy is within ±10%, but the experiment falsifies the hypothesis only for errors greater than ±15%, leaving errors between 10% and 15% inconsistent with the claim but non-falsifying.
The claimed efficiency gain is at least 10×, but the experiment falsifies only gains below 5×, leaving a 5× to 10× result that misses the claim without falsifying it.
